source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ τίνα τρόπον φησὶν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος ὅτι εἰ δ᾿ οὖν τό γε τοσοῦτον ὤφειλεν εἰς ἐπίδειξιν θεότητος, ἀπὸ τοῦ σκόλοπος γοῦν εὐθὺς ἀφανὴς γενέσθαι. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ δοκεῖ μοι ὅμοιον εἶναι τῷ λόγῳ τῶν ἀντιδιατασσόντων τῇ προνοίᾳ καὶ διαγραφόντων ἑαυτοῖς ἕτερα παρὰ τὰ ὄντα καὶ λεγόντων ὅτι βέλτιον ἦν, εἰ οὕτως εἶχεν ὁ κόσμος, ὡς διεγράψαμεν. ὅπου μὲν γὰρ δυνατὰ διαγράφουσιν, ἐλέγχονται χείρονα ποιοῦντες τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς καὶ τῇ διαγραφῇ αὐτῶν τὸν κόσμον, ὅπου δὲ δοκοῦσι μὴ χείρονα ἀναζωγραφεῖν τῶν ὄντων, ἀποδείκνυνται τὰ τῇ φύσει ἀδύνατα βουλόμενοι· ὡς ἑκατέρως αὐτοὺς καταγελάστους εἶναι. καὶ ἐνθάδε τοίνυν ὅτι μὲν οὐκ ἀδύνατον ἥξειν ὡς ἐν τῇ θειοτέρᾳ φύσει, ἵν᾿ ὅτε βούληται ἀφανὴς γένηται, καὶ αὐτόθεν μὲν δῆλον σαφὲς δὲ καὶ ἐκ τῶν γεγραμμένων περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῖς μὴ τινὰ μὲν τῶν γεγραμμένων προσιεμένοις, ἵνα κατηγορήσωσι τοῦ λόγου, τινὰ δὲ πλάσματα οἰομένοις τυγχάνειν. γέγραπται δὲ ἐν τῷ κατὰ Λουκᾶν ὅτι μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν „λαβὼν τὸν ἄρτον·“ ὁ Ἰησοῦς „εὐλόγησε καὶ κλάσας ἐπεδίδου“ τῷ Σίμωνι καὶ τῷ Κλεόπᾳ· λαβόντων δ᾿ αὐτῶν τὸν ἄρτον „διηνοίχθησαν αὐτῶν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ, καὶ ἐπέγνωσαν αὐτόν· καὶ αὐτὸς ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν.“
pass_a_gloss: Let us see in what manner (τίνα τρόπον) the Jew in Celsus says that: 'but if anyway (εἰ δ᾿ οὖν) he was bound (ὤφειλεν) [to do] at least so much (τό γε τοσοῦτον) for a display (ἐπίδειξις) of divinity (θεότης), at least (γοῦν) from the stake (σκόλοψ) [he should] at once (εὐθύς) become invisible (ἀφανής).' And this too seems to me like the argument (λόγος) of those who array themselves against providence (πρόνοια) and sketch out (διαγραφόντων) for themselves other things beside the existing (τὰ ὄντα), and say that it was better (βέλτιον) if the world (κόσμος) were thus as we sketched. For where they sketch possible things (δυνατά), they are refuted (ἐλέγχονται) as making the world worse (χείρονα) as far as on themselves and by their sketch (διαγραφή); and where they seem to paint anew (ἀναζωγραφεῖν) things not worse than the existing, they are shown wishing things impossible by nature; so that either way (ἑκατέρως) they are laughable (καταγέλαστοι). And here then, that it was not impossible as in the more divine nature (θειοτέρα φύσις), so that whenever he wishes (βούληται) he becomes invisible, is both clear from the thing itself (αὐτόθεν) and plain also from the things written about him, to those who do not admit some of the writings in order to accuse (κατηγορήσωσι) the word (λόγος), and suppose (οἰομένοις) others to be fictions (πλάσματα). And it is written in the [Gospel] according to Luke that after the resurrection Jesus 'taking the bread blessed (εὐλόγησε) and breaking (κλάσας) was handing (ἐπεδίδου)' to Simon and Cleopas; and when they took the bread, 'their eyes were opened up (διηνοίχθησαν), and they recognised (ἐπέγνωσαν) him; and he became unseen (ἄφαντος) from them.'
pass_b_english: Let us see how Celsus’s Jew puts it: “In any case, to display his divinity he ought at least to have done this much: to vanish from the stake at once.” This too seems to me like the argument of those who set themselves against providence, who sketch for themselves things other than what exists, and say, “It would have been better if the world were as we have sketched it.” Where what they sketch is possible, they are shown to be making the world worse, so far as it lies with them and their sketch; and where they seem to be painting something not worse than what exists, they are shown to want what is impossible by nature. So either way they are ridiculous.

Here too, then, that it was not impossible for him, as one of a more divine nature, to become invisible whenever he wished, is clear in itself. It is plain also from what is written about him, to anyone except those who accept some of the writings in order to attack the word, and think others are fictions. Now it is written in the Gospel according to Luke that after the resurrection Jesus “took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it” to Simon and Cleopas; and when they had taken the bread, “their eyes were opened, and they recognised him; and he vanished from their sight” (Luke 24:30–31).

choices.term: εἰ δ᾿ οὖν τό γε τοσοῦτον ὤφειλεν
choices.why: Jew's words: εἰ δ᾿ οὖν τό γε τοσοῦτον ὤφειλεν... ἀφανὴς γενέσθαι corrected; τοσοῦτον is the object explained by the infinitive, not a condition ('In any case, to display his divinity he ought at least to have done this much: to vanish from the stake at once').
Negated participles (μὴ ... προσιεμένοις ... οἰομένοις) recast as 'to anyone except those who accept some ... and think others are fictions', removing the ambiguity of 'does not accept some'.
κατηγορήσωσι: 'accuse' -> 'attack'; γέγραπται δέ: 'For' -> 'Now'; Luke 24:30 list smoothed.

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

notes: Translated from the Greek of the staged Koetschau row only; Crombie (ANF) and Chadwick were not used.
Independent clause review: every clause checked; verdict pass.
Scripture citations sit inline beside the clause in Pass B.
2.68: the copy-text 'οὐκ ἀδύνατον ἥξειν' looks corrupt and is rendered by its evident sense. The edition apparatus was not available to check.

translator_notes: Speaker: ‘ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος’ rendered ‘Celsus’s Jew’; his words in double quotation marks. ‘σκόλοψ’ (stake, pale) is Celsus’s word, distinct from ‘σταυρός’ (cross) used by Origen in 2.69; rendered ‘stake’ throughout. ‘εἰ δ᾿ οὖν τό γε τοσοῦτον ὤφειλεν’ is elliptical (‘if anyway he had to do at least this much’); rendered ‘In any case, to display his divinity he ought at least to have done this much: to vanish from the stake at once’. The quoted sentence of the critics of providence (‘it would have been better...’) is a reported generic objection, set in quotation marks as direct speech in the Greek (‘λεγόντων ὅτι... ὡς διεγράψαμεν’, first person). Doubtful reading: ‘οὐκ ἀδύνατον ἥξειν ὡς ἐν τῇ θειοτέρᾳ φύσει’ does not construe cleanly (‘ἥξειν’, ‘would come’, seems corrupt; an infinitive like ‘ἦν αὐτῷ’ or similar is expected); rendered by the evident sense ‘it was not impossible for him, as one of a more divine nature, to become invisible whenever he wished’. ‘μὴ... προσιεμένοις..., ... οἰομένοις’: the negative governs both participles, describing readers who do not pick and choose (accept some texts to attack, dismiss others as fiction); ‘ὁ λόγος’ = the Christian word/teaching, lowercase as in 2.66. Luke 24:30-31 is quoted closely; ‘ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν’ rendered ‘vanished from their sight’. Origen names the companion of Cleopas ‘Simon’ (not named in Luke 24:18; compare Luke 24:34, ‘he has appeared to Simon’); kept as he gives it. Reviewer: ‘εἰ δ᾿ οὖν’ read as ‘in any case / failing that’; ‘τό γε τοσοῦτον’ is the object of ‘ὤφειλεν’ and is spelled out by ‘ἀφανὴς γενέσθαι’. The ‘μὴ’ clause is rendered with ‘anyone except those who...’ so the negation covers both participles without ambiguity.
